The second bottle came three days after the first, carried in on a gentle morning tide. Elias found it at sunrise, nestled in a bed of bladderwrack as if placed there by hand. Same glass, same red wax seal, same cramped handwriting inside.

"October 19th — the old pier at Harrowby will collapse during the school trip. A child will fall through. She will not surface unless someone enters the water from the east stairs."

Elias didn't laugh this time.

He spent October 18th pacing the lighthouse gallery, arguing with himself. It was coincidence. It had to be coincidence. The Mary Ellen was old, everyone knew she'd capsize eventually. But the date, the boat's name, the location — those weren't coincidence. Those were precision. And precision, Elias knew from a lifetime of keeping the light, was the opposite of chance.

At nine in the morning on October 19th, he stationed himself at the east stairs of the old pier. He told himself he was being ridiculous. He told himself that right up until the timber cracked like a rifle shot and a girl in a red coat plunged through the gap into the black water below.

He was in before the scream finished echoing off the harbor wall. The October sea hit like poured concrete — every nerve screaming to surface, to retreat. He dove anyway, hands sweeping through murk until his fingers caught netting, then fabric, then a small arm rigid with panic. The girl weighed nothing and everything. He kicked upward with her clutched to his chest, lungs burning, and broke the surface to a wall of noise — shouts, crying, the groan of splitting wood.

Hands reached down from the pier and hauled them both out. The girl — Rosie Calder, seven years old, red coat now black with water — coughed, screamed for her mother, and lived.

By afternoon, Elias Mercer was the talk of Harrowby. The reclusive lighthouse keeper who'd saved little Rosie Calder. The harbor master, a broad man called Tom Vane, shook his hand so hard Elias thought his shoulder would dislocate.

"How'd you know to be there?" Tom asked, eyes narrowing just slightly.

"Luck," Elias said. The word tasted like rust.

The third bottle arrived the next morning. This one stopped his breath:

"October 31st — Harvest Festival night. Fire in the town hall. Starts in the kitchen store cupboard. Seventeen people inside. The doors jam."

Elias went to Tom Vane first. He sat in the harbor master's office, the smell of diesel and rope thick in the air, and explained everything — the bottles, the predictions, all of it. Tom listened with his arms crossed, then rubbed his face with both hands.

"Elias. You've been alone up in that tower too long, mate."

He tried the constable next. Then the pub landlord, who poured him a pity pint and changed the subject. Same answer everywhere, delivered with varying degrees of kindness. The crazy lighthouse keeper and his messages from the sea.

It was Tom's daughter who found him sitting on the harbor wall that evening, boots dangling over the water, the note smoothed flat on his knee. Marina Vane was twenty-six, sharp-featured, practical as a tide table. She ran the marine supply shop and had no patience for nonsense.

"My father says you've lost it," she said, sitting beside him uninvited.

"Your father might be right."

She held out her hand. "Show me the note."

He handed it over. She read it once, quickly, then again slowly. Turned it over. Held the paper up to the fading light as if checking for a watermark. Then she looked at him — really looked, the way you look at a locked door when you're deciding whether to kick it in.

"The first prediction — the Mary Ellen. Where exactly did the note say it would happen?"

"Harbor mouth. Two aboard. Someone on the north jetty throws a line."

"And the pier — it said east stairs specifically?"

"Word for word."

Marina folded the note carefully and handed it back. "I don't believe in prophecy," she said. "But I believe in patterns. And you've got a pattern. So what's the plan for the town hall?"
